Fulness
FOOL-nes
n.
From full + -ness. Renders the Greek plērōma, “that which fills, completion, fulness,” and plousios-family riches-of words; and the Hebrew mālē’, “to be full,” and shalom in its sense of completeness.

📖 Biblical Definition

Fulness in Scripture is one of the deepest Christological and ecclesiological substantives, governing several great doctrinal claims. First, the fulness of God is in Christ bodily: for it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell; for in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The Christ in whom the church places her trust is no diminished mediator but the One in whom the entire divine fulness has taken residence in the incarnation. Second, the fulness of Christ is given to the church: and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all. The church is named in the staggering category of Christ’s own fulness; she is what fills Him out in His mediatorial reign over creation, even as He Himself is full of the Godhead. Third, the church is being grown into the measure of Christ’s fulness: till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ. The fulness already given (in union with Christ) is to be progressively realized in the church’s growth toward the maturity of her Head. Fourth, the fulness of times is the appointed historical hour at which God brought His redemptive purposes to their climax: but when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law; that in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ. History is not random; it ripens to its appointed fulness in Christ. Fifth, the fulness of the Gentiles and of Israel are paired in Rom 11 as the great eschatological ingatherings: blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved. Fulness is therefore the verb of completion brought into substantive form: completion of the divine indwelling in Christ; completion of Christ’s mediatorial body in the church; completion of the church’s maturation into her Head; completion of God’s historical purposes in the appointed hour; completion of the redemptive gathering of Gentile and Jew alike. The fulness category gathers up the whole scope of God’s saving work and sets it forth as the sufficient, complete, exhaustive answer of God to every emptiness sin produced.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FULNESS as the state of being filled so as to leave no part vacant; the state of abounding or being in great plenty; in theology, the entirety of divine attributes dwelling in Christ.

expand to see more

FULNESS, n. — 1. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant. 2. The state of abounding or being in great plenty. 3. Completeness; the state of being full or fully completed. 4. Largeness; extent; vastness. 5. In theology, the entirety of divine attributes dwelling in Christ (Col 1:19; 2:9); the completeness of the appointed times (Gal 4:4).

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Ephesians 1:22-23 — "And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all."

Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

Ephesians 4:13 — "Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The doctrine of fulness is corrupted, on one side, by the diminished-Christ register of liberal critical scholarship that strips Christ of the divine fulness Colossians explicitly affirms—and on the other by the experiential register that treats fulness of the Spirit as a privileged second-blessing rather than as the ordinary regenerate life applied to the body of Christ.

expand to see more

Liberal critical traditions corrupt fulness by stripping Christ of the divine fulness Colossians and Ephesians explicitly affirm. The high Christology of in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily is treated as later theological development to be peeled away from a more modest historical Jesus; the cosmic Christ of the fulness of him that filleth all in all is replaced by a wisdom teacher whose authority is bracketed and whose claims are domesticated. The recovery is the recovery of the text’s plain claim. The Christ the apostles announce is the One in whom the entire divine fulness has taken residence; any diminishment of this Christ is the loss of the Christ the New Testament actually delivers. The fulness category is not a peripheral New Testament idea but a structural one—and stripping it produces a different Christ, a different church, and a different gospel.

The experiential corruption is the treatment of fulness of the Spirit as a privileged second-blessing experience available only to a subset of believers, often marked by particular spiritual phenomena, rather than as the ordinary regenerate life applied to the whole body of Christ. The New Testament does speak of being filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18) and being full of the Holy Ghost (Acts 6:3; 11:24), and these are realities to be sought and known. But the structural category of fulness in Ephesians 1, Colossians 1-2, and Galatians 4 is not a privileged-elite experience; it is the foundational reality of every believer’s union with the Christ in whom all fulness dwells. The recovery is to hold both: the foundational fulness of every believer in Christ (which grounds all assurance), and the practical, daily, ongoing fulness of the Spirit (which is sought, walked in, and to be characteristic of every Christian, not a privileged subset). Both together display the doctrine the New Testament actually teaches—and the church that holds both is the church that knows the sufficient, complete, exhaustive answer of God in Christ to every emptiness sin produced.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek plērōma (that which fills, completion, fulness) and the verb plēroō (to fill); Hebrew mālē’ (to be full) and shalom (completeness)—the Christological and ecclesiological category of completion in Christ, by whom all the fulness of God indwells the church through union with Him.

expand to see more

Greek plērōma (G4138) — that which fills, completion, fulness (the great Christological substantive; Col 1:19; 2:9; Eph 1:23; 3:19; 4:13).

Greek plēroō (G4137) — to fill up, complete, fulfill (the cognate verb).

Hebrew mālē’ (H4390) — to be full, to fill.

Hebrew mālō’ (H4393) — fulness (the noun; “the earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof”).

Usage

"For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily—the high Christology of Colossians 2:9 is the church’s decisive claim about her Lord."

"The church is named in the staggering category of Christ’s own fulness—his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all."

"When the fulness of the time was come—history ripens to its appointed fulness in Christ; the redemptive hour was not random but ordained."
